direct_answer:
BASF states it conducted a double materiality assessment in accordance with ESRS for the first time in 2024, building on prior assessments but with increased granularity and documentation, and plans to update it annually [Source 1]. The assessment was performed in three steps: (1) compiling a list of potential sustainability matters relevant to BASF’s business/customer industries and stakeholder groups, with particular attention to higher-risk areas of business/value chains; the assessment was carried out at Group level along the value chain [Source 1]. (2) considering stakeholder interests via direct inputs (e.g., Advisory Councils, BASF Civil Society Forum, multistakeholder networks) and indirect inputs (e.g., big data analyses of customer and capital market interests), and working with in-house experts plus selected stakeholders in the Nature and Human Rights Advisory Councils to identify/validate risks and opportunities linked to impacts and dependencies; BASF also drew on its Group-wide opportunity and risk management and expert review of impacts/dependencies to identify additional risks/opportunities [Source 1]. (3) scoring impacts, risks and opportunities using predetermined criteria on a 5-point scale and classifying them as material when exceeding defined thresholds; impacts were assessed for severity/scale/scope (and irremediability for negative impacts) and likelihood for potential impacts; opportunities/risks were assessed for financial magnitude and likelihood; the assessment was reviewed iteratively by interdisciplinary experts and risk-reporting experts, and governance bodies (Board of Executive Directors, Supervisory Board, Joint Works Council, Works Council Europe) were informed of process and outcome [Source 3]. After identifying material IROs, BASF mapped them to ESRS topic/subtopic/sub-subtopic (per ESRS 1 AR 16) and assessed “materiality of information” at disclosure requirement/data point level using EFRAG criteria (“decision-usefulness” and “stakeholder relevance”) [Source 4].

The retrieved passages do not provide a consolidated list of sustainability matters that are material from both an impact and a financial perspective (i.e., “double material” topics). BASF does indicate that (a) its main impacts relate to climate change, other environmental matters (emissions to air, water and biodiversity) and its own workforce [Source 2], (b) Biodiversity and Ecosystems was defined as material [Source 8], (c) topics in Own Workforce were defined as material [Source 12], and (d) ESRS S4 Consumers and End Users was assessed as not material [Source 2]. However, the passages do not explicitly state which topics are material in both dimensions (impact and financial) at topic level; they only note generally that identified opportunities and risks have financial effects and give one example of financial effects arising from a risk under S3 Affected Communities [Source 2].
compliance_rationale: Process description is well evidenced (steps, stakeholder inputs, scoring/thresholds, impact and financial risk/opportunity criteria, value-chain scope, governance review) [Sources 1, 3, 4]. However, the evidence provided does not include an explicit identification of which sustainability matters are material from both impact and financial perspectives; only partial topic-level materiality statements (e.g., E4 and Own Workforce material; S4 not material) and a general statement about financial effects plus one S3 example are available [Sources 2, 8, 12].
disclosure_gaps: Explicit list of sustainability matters that are material from both impact and financial perspectives (double material) at ESRS topic/subtopic level is not provided in the retrieved passages.
Clear topic-by-topic conclusion distinguishing impact materiality vs financial materiality (and their interdependencies) is not shown in the retrieved passages.
Quantitative/qualitative thresholds used (numerical values) for determining materiality are not disclosed in the retrieved passages (only that thresholds exist and a 5-point scale was used).

Description of how due diligence outcomes specifically informed the materiality assessment is not explicitly evidenced in the retrieved passages (beyond references to risk management and expert/stakeholder inputs).
key_findings: BASF performed an ESRS-aligned double materiality assessment for the first time in 2024, at Group level along the value chain, and intends annual updates [Source 1].

Stakeholder interests were incorporated through direct engagement formats (Advisory Councils, Civil Society Forum, multistakeholder networks) and indirect inputs (big data analyses of customer/capital market interests); selected stakeholders in Nature and Human Rights Advisory Councils helped identify/validate risks and opportunities linked to impacts and dependencies [Source 1].

Impacts, risks and opportunities were scored on a 5-point scale against predetermined criteria and deemed material when exceeding thresholds; impacts were assessed by severity/scale/scope (plus irremediability for negative impacts) and likelihood for potential impacts; risks/opportunities were assessed by financial magnitude and likelihood [Source 3].

Material IROs were mapped to ESRS topics/subtopics/sub-subtopics and BASF assessed materiality of information at disclosure requirement/data point level using EFRAG criteria (decision-usefulness and stakeholder relevance) [Source 4].
Biodiversity and Ecosystems (E4) and Own Workforce topics were defined as material; Consumers and End Users (S4) was not material [Sources 8, 12, 2].

BASF notes its main impacts relate to climate change, other environmental matters (including biodiversity) and its workforce; it also notes financial effects from identified opportunities/risks and cites one instance of financial effects linked to an S3 Affected Communities risk [Source 2].
